Continuous commands scale this gradient by a learned positive gain, while discrete commands use finite differences of the same scalar. This yields a hybrid policy without a separate action head or iterative search. Fitting demonstration progress values alone does not ensure that action gradients align with expert commands. PPP trains the induced commands by imitation and uses double backpropagation for the continuous gradient readout to shape the field's local control geometry. Demonstration timing calibrates field values on observed states without additional annotation. The continuous readout remains learnable without progress labels but these timing-derived targets support progress monitoring during execution. Experiments in simulated and real robot manipulation show that PPP outperforms behavioral cloning under a shared architecture.

arxiv:2611.22407.title: ROSMonitoring in Action: Runtime Monitoring and Enforcement for ROS 2 Actions
arxiv:2611.22407.abstract: Robotic applications often rely on long-running operations, such as navigation, manipulation, and inspection, which in ROS~2 are commonly implemented as actions. Unlike topics and services, actions involve a structured lifecycle comprising goal submission and acceptance, feedback, status updates, result retrieval, and cancellation. Existing versions of ROSMonitoring support topics and services, but do not reconstruct this lifecycle or expose action-level events to a runtime-verification oracle. In this paper, we extend ROSMonitoring with runtime monitoring and enforcement for ROS~2 actions. Actions are declared directly in the monitoring configuration and automatically instrumented through the underlying ROS~2 communication endpoints. The generated monitor reconstructs action-level events, correlates them through goal identifiers, maintains the state of active goals, and translates violations into protocol-aware enforcement operations. These include goal rejection, cancellation, message suppression, and protocol-compliant responses generated directly by the monitor when the original communication cannot be forwarded. We evaluate the implementation through controlled stress tests that vary the number of action invocations, workload size, and clientâserver topology. The results show approximately linear growth in monitoring cost with repeated action invocations under a fixed workload, while larger action workloads and a greater number of configured clientâserver pairs introduce additional overhead. These results characterise the scaling behaviour of the current implementation under the tested sequential workloads while highlighting the main performance limitations of the current synchronous implementation.

arxiv:2611.22395.title: CoBoVLA: Decoupling Language from Action with Discrete Codes for Robust and Interpretable Robot Manipulation
arxiv:2611.22395.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve high success rates on the LIBERO benchmark but remain sensitive to paraphrasing. Existing VLAs ranging from 0.6B to 7.5B parameters experience a 22-52 point performance drop on LIBERO-Para while SmolVLA exhibits an even larger decline, from 83\% to 8\%. Because most VLAs jointly learn language understanding and action generation, it is difficult to determine whether a failure originates from misunderstanding an instruction or executing it incorrectly. To address these challenges, we introduce CoBoVLA, or CodeBookVLA, a 250M-parameter VLA that decouples language understanding, planning, and control through learned discrete interpretable codes. A text encoder maps the instructions to shared step codes, which a visual planner then converts into action code sequences executed by a language-independent actor. This design improves robustness to instruction paraphrasing while allowing failures to be traced to individual stages. It also enables efficient real-time control on resource-constrained hardware by encoding instructions only once and using compact discrete representations to keep each component lightweight. CoBoVLA achieves 91.4\% success on LIBERO-Goal, compared with 82.8\% for SmolVLA, under a matched protocol, with 17 ms per control step latency. On LIBERO-Para, it achieves 81.1\% across 4,092 unseen paraphrases and 78.5\% on matched episodes, compared with 36.5\% for SmolVLA LoRA fine-tuned on paraphrases. Without two-step demonstrations, CoBoVLA completes 48.8\% of 160 free-form two-step tasks. Finally, success reaches 91\% when instructions are correctly encoded but falls to 27.2\% otherwise, identifying language understanding as the main source of remaining failures. Together, these results demonstrate that decoupling language understanding and control can improve instruction robustness while making VLA failures easier to diagnose.
arxiv:2611.22395.authors: Mehul Arora, Dhruv Agarwal, Ambuj Agrawal

arxiv:2611.22388.title: Hidden Variables Behind Real-Robot Data Quality: Lessons from Hundreds of Thousands of Hours
arxiv:2611.22388.abstract: As real-robot data collection scales, collection-system design shapes both operator efficiency and the behaviors learned by robot policies. Workspace limitations, control-interface friction, and latency can introduce pauses, detours, and corrective motions into otherwise successful demonstrations. We investigate these effects across embodiment, teleoperation control, and data consistency, combining a kinematic study of 25 dual-arm robots, controlled teleoperation experiments, and real-robot evaluation of fine-tuned $π_{0.5}$ policies. The embodiment study shows that positional reachability overstates orientation-aware task coverage and that modest shoulder motion can substantially expand the effective workspace. Teleoperation experiments show that parallelizing body-part control reduces task completion time by 43-53%, while compliant control improves success and reduces peak contact forces on constrained and contact-rich tasks. Policy-learning experiments show that demonstrations must capture the visual information underlying action choices: active-search demonstrations improve arm-selection accuracy from chance (50%) to 100%. Calibration experiments reveal that mixed-calibration training data remain usable in our tested configurations when an inference-aligned subset is retained, whereas inference-time miscalibration causes all 30 trials to fail. Policies also retain approximately 90% of the extra path length in detour-contaminated demonstrations, showing how inefficient operator motions persist in learned behavior. Together, these findings connect collection-system design to demonstration quality and downstream policy execution. They motivate evaluating effective workspace, control efficiency, observation completeness, calibration alignment, and motion quality before scaling collection, and addressing system-induced compensations at their source.
arxiv:2611.22388.authors: Maniformer Real-World Manipulation Team, Che Tsang Calvin, Xingyu Chen, Bowen Jiang, Naixiang Gao, Xiongfeng Cai, Enlin Gu, Ruiying Li, Peize Li, Mianrui Zhu, Haomiao Zhang, Xin He, Minhui Yu, Jun Zhao, Zihao Zhu, Yang Chen, Jingmei Jin, Keru Zhou, Chen Wang, Chang Zhou, Zhiwen Hou, Di Yang, Wenjun Sun, Fan Yang, Liyan Zhang, Yi Lu, Haojun Ma, Jun Zhu, Pengxin Zha, Zhaosheng Wang, Xin Zhao, Xindong He, Chiming Liu, Jianheng Song, Jiayao Ma, Maoqing Yao, Guanghui Ren, Qian Wang, Wei Shan, Yang Yang, Li Liu, Wenhao Wang

arxiv:2611.22275.title: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration
arxiv:2611.22275.abstract: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.
arxiv:2611.22275.authors: Ting-Hsuan Chen, Siheng Zhao, Han Jiang, Qi Pan, Louison Lu, Jiaheng Luo, Henghui Bao, Yiyu Chen, Quan Nguyen, Yue Wang

arxiv:2611.22691.title: Making the World React Realistically: A Closed-Loop Interactive World Model for Autonomous Driving
arxiv:2611.22691.abstract: World models (WMs) generate driving scenarios beyond recorded logs, enabling the training and evaluation of autonomous driving systems in unseen interactions. However, existing WMs struggle to ensure both behavioral realism and visual fidelity, since they overlook the relationship between vehicle interactions and the ego visual observations. We propose a closed-loop interactive WM that couples behavior modeling and visual rendering. First, imitation-learned background-vehicle (BV) policies are fine-tuned with multi-agent reinforcement learning in the closed loop against an end-to-end ego planner that reacts to the rendered images, so that their interaction behaviors match those in real logs. Second, the viewpoints exposed by these interactions guide a per-Gaussian diagnosis of each 3D Gaussian vehicle asset, which attenuates view-dependent colors on under-observed Gaussians and fills never-observed surfaces with generated Gaussians, while preserving the observed appearance. Third, signal lights are rendered according to the driving intentions of the vehicles, by an editor that learns the light states unobserved for a vehicle through counterfactual fine-tuning with a light-state classifier. On long-tail closed-loop scenarios, our method reduces the divergence from real-world interaction behaviors by 85% and improves novel-view vehicle PSNR by 2.0dB over the state-of-the-art WM. The significance of BV light signaling in WMs is shown, as the rendered signal lights conveying BV driving intentions indirectly impact ego driving behaviors in a quarter of the scenarios.
arxiv:2611.22691.authors: Jia Hu, Yang Chang, Panqu Wang, Zhijun Fu, Chang Liu, Changjian Yu, Jintao Lai

arxiv:2611.22367.title: FailureGen: Scalable Robot Failure Data Generation with World Models
arxiv:2611.22367.abstract: Robot failures are difficult to collect at scale, limiting the range of failure scenarios represented in robot learning datasets. We present FailureGen, a method for generating synthetic videos with temporal event annotations by reusing action trajectories from recorded failures. The method comprises four stages: (1) fine-tuning an action-conditioned Cosmos world model on successful and failed real executions; (2) annotating source recordings to identify failure-associated donor segments and compatible successful hosts; (3) transferring donor motion into host contexts, with optional spatial offsets, to generate continuous video rollouts; and (4) annotating and filtering the generated samples according to observed events and visual quality. We study two implementations with different tasks and robot configurations, with visual failure detection serving as one downstream application. In a preliminary comparison, a detector trained on real and generated data achieves an average precision of 0.51, compared with 0.41 using real data alone, and detects 33 of 36 failure intervals, compared with 28 of 36. By reusing observed failures in additional contexts, FailureGen expands the data available for studying robot failures and developing downstream learning methods.
arxiv:2611.22367.authors: Akul Santhosh, Chaitra Sathe, Aastha Jhunjhunwala

arxiv:2611.22258.title: ALERT: Extending Humanoid Motion Trackers with a General and Lightweight Human Avoidance Pipeline
arxiv:2611.22258.abstract: Whole-body motion tracking has enabled humanoid dancing, athletic motions, and teleoperation, providing a foundation for capability demonstrations and manipulation data collection. However, existing tracking policies lack awareness of nearby humans and proactive avoidance capabilities, while motion substitution and local constraint-based corrections may compromise reference motion integrity and tracking continuity. We propose ALERT, a general lightweight pipeline for extending motion tracking to shared human-robot environments. Through lightweight adaptation, it integrates human perception and proactive avoidance into pretrained tracking policies, balancing avoidance demands with reference motion tracking while preserving existing motion capabilities. Simulation and real-world experiments across tracking backbones demonstrate reliable collision-free execution through localized human avoidance, preserving whole-body coordination and enabling rapid recovery of reference tracking, while retaining the ability of pretrained policies to track unseen motions.
arxiv:2611.22258.authors: Zhaoyang Li, Chiyu Zhang, Chengxin Xu, Peng Yang, Zhonghao Guo, Wanting Li, Ziyu Chen

arxiv:2611.22132.title: DailyBrick: Language-Guided Synthesis of Brick Assembly Instructions
arxiv:2611.22132.abstract: Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (https://SpatialAgent.github.io/DailyBrick/).
arxiv:2611.22132.authors: Hang Zhang, Qijian Tian, Yuan Xie, Xuhong Wang, Xin Tan

arxiv:2611.22001.title: DreamFAR: Real-Time and Long-Horizon Interaction with Diverse Objects
arxiv:2611.22001.abstract: World models have shown great potential in serving as a simulator for robot manipulation. However, existing models are either fit to a single environment or lack ability to simulate long-horizon contact-rich events. We present DreamFAR, a world model whose dynamics model is trained from scratch on a large robot-native teleoperation dataset, with no internet-video pretraining. We present an architecture and learning recipe designed for training on robot-native data. DreamFAR is significantly smaller than the high-performance video generation models, yet shows better understanding of contact and causality, and runs 10 FPS on a commercial GPU. Experimentally, DreamFAR significantly outperforms existing models in predicting the long-horizon future. We further demonstrate various applications where DreamFAR can be used, including policy evaluation and mixed-data co-training. Project page: https://www.yimingdou.com/DreamFAR/
arxiv:2611.22001.authors: Yiming Dou, Botao He, Antonio Loquercio, Andrew Owens, Jitendra Malik, Sumedh Anand Sontakke, Ruoshi Liu

arxiv:2611.21938.title: HubEgo-100K: In-the-Wild Egocentric Video of Skilled Work for Robot Learning
arxiv:2611.21938.abstract: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing egocentric video, however, mostly shows daily-life activity and contains little skilled work in real workplaces. We present HubEgo-100K, a dataset built for diversity. This version of the paper covers the first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from one head-mounted phone camera. In v1.0, 12,227 contributors record their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments (each one contributor's own setting of one type, such as their kitchen or workshop) across 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types and 35 action families, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. The release comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations, in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0. We measure diversity along each axis, show that inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing, and relate the measurements to published evidence on six data properties tied to policy performance, including hand visibility and inertial sensing. We also document collection, curation, privacy measures and data format, and provide a datasheet. Later versions of this paper will add benchmarks and cover further releases toward 100,000 hours.
arxiv:2611.21938.authors: Javad Amirian, Armin Kiani, Loïc Schaeffer, Tim Sprecher, Mohamed Taha, Karthik Yadati

arxiv:2611.21919.title: ALOHA Lightning: Learning Fast and Precise Manipulation
arxiv:2611.21919.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has enabled robots to acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, but learned policies typically execute far slower than ordinary humans. This speed gap is mainly due to lack of an interface for collecting demonstration data at high speed, and the difficulty in training policies that can robustly execute high-speed motions. In this paper, we present ALOHA Lightning (Flash ALOHA), a system for learning fast and precise robotic manipulation. Our system uses kinesthetic teaching to intuitively collect near-human-speed demonstrations on a backdrivable bimanual platform, yielding natural and fast trajectories. We also present a learning pipeline that enables smooth high-speed execution through test-time action smoothing and aligns the visual data distribution between data collection and deployment with masking. Given 50 demonstrations for each task, ALOHA Lightning autonomously completes bimanual tasks such as ball tossing and catching, folding shorts, battery insertion, and bussing tables for over 80% success rates while close to human speed. Project website: https://flash-aloha.github.io/
arxiv:2611.21919.authors: John Hua Yao. Qi Wu, Yihuai Gao, Chelsea Finn, Zipeng Fu

arxiv:2611.21908.title: From Human Videos to Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Data: Confidence-Guided RL Refinement of Video Priors
arxiv:2611.21908.abstract: Collecting demonstrations for bimanual dexterous manipulation is costly, motivating the use of human videos as a source of robot training data. However, uncertainty in video-derived motion estimates and differences between human and robot embodiments make direct motion transfer challenging. In this work, we introduce PriDex, a framework that transforms human-video Priors into executable robot Dexterous manipulation demonstrations through reinforcement learning in simulation. PriDex preserves task-relevant interaction structure while allowing embodiment-specific behavior to be regenerated for the robot. Human-object interactions provide affordance cues for selecting task-relevant, robot-specific grasps from geometry-based candidates. For motion refinement, object trajectories provide a task-level reference, while relative bimanual wrist trajectories offer complementary guidance for coordinated motion. Since object-motion estimates can become unreliable under occlusion or visual ambiguity, PriDex uses object-motion confidence to adaptively balance these two priors, emphasizing object-level guidance when confidence is high and increasing the contribution of wrist-level guidance as confidence decreases. Reinforcement learning refines these video-derived priors under the robot's kinematic and physical constraints, and the resulting policies are rolled out to generate robot demonstrations for training a vision-based diffusion policy. We evaluate PriDex on four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, including pouring, sweeping into a dustpan, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate cleaning, assessing both simulation-based robot data generation and downstream visuomotor policy learning.
arxiv:2611.21908.authors: Yanghong Liu, Yang Chen, Kailang Xu, Bang Du, Feiyang Yang, Jiawei Xia, Zhengtao Yao, Yubiao Zhang, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Ruihai Wu, Wei Zhan

arxiv:2611.22883.title: Fly as Instructed: Refining World-Action Policies for UAV Vision-Language Navigation
arxiv:2611.22883.abstract: Natural language-guided UAV navigation enables intuitive human-robot interaction and flexible autonomous flight in complex environments. However, reliable navigation requires accurate instruction following, continuous task progress tracking, and safe obstacle avoidance, which remain challenging for existing world-action models that primarily focus on action prediction. To address these limitations, we propose a world-action learning framework that integrates three complementary mechanisms: a language-conditioned action interface with targeted post-training for instruction-responsive motion, recurrent instruction-consumption prediction to track task progress and determine termination, and Gaussian-scene post-training to enhance obstacle avoidance through trajectory imitation and differentiable geometric feedback. Closed-loop evaluations and ablation studies demonstrate improvements in sequential task completion, safe goal reaching, and timely termination. Furthermore, direct one-step denoising reduces inference overhead, and real-world indoor and outdoor flights validate the framework's effectiveness.
arxiv:2611.22883.authors: Zhexuan Zhou, Yanke Sun, Yuhan Zong, Youmin Gong, Jie Mei

arxiv:2611.22453.title: VoxelSBFL: Voxel-Level Spectrum-Based Failure Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models
arxiv:2611.22453.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots. Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.
arxiv:2611.22453.authors: Arusa Kanwal, Pablo Valle, Paola Roggero, Miren Illarramendi, Shaukat Ali, Aitor Arrieta

arxiv:2611.22356.title: SR-VLA: Stall-Reduced VLA Execution via Predicted-Input Lookahead and Selective KV Cache Repair
arxiv:2611.22356.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur control stalls when inference blocks the next action chunk. Asynchronous early inference can hide latency, but its results may be inconsistent with the arriving actual inputs. Unconditional reuse risks acting on mismatched inputs, whereas full recomputation discards useful precomputation. We propose SR-VLA, combining predicted-input lookahead with selective KV cache repair. During current chunk execution, a lightweight action-conditioned predictor generates next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state. These predictions, together with the task instruction, drive the frozen VLA to precompute a speculative KV cache and action chunk. After real inputs are available to VLA, predicted--real differences and task conditions determine whether to accept the action chunk or trigger selective KV repair. On LIBERO, SR-VLA achieves $2.67\times$ and $1.27\times$ query speedups over the respective synchronous $π_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA-OFT baselines, while maintaining competitive average task success rates. Under target-motion perturbation, success remains baseline-comparable, with $1.52\times$--$1.93\times$ query speedup.
arxiv:2611.22356.authors: Tao Zhang, Yi Zhong, Jinhao Ruan, Yipeng Gao, Linfeng Zhong, Youming Yang, Yuan Wang

arxiv:2611.22077.title: ReLAP: Latent Action Pretraining through Recurrent Video Prediction in JEPA Space
arxiv:2611.22077.abstract: Videos provide a rich source of physical interaction for learning robot behavior without action annotations, yet effective latent actions must capture not only local transitions but also how those transitions evolve over time. We introduce ReLAP, a latent-action pretraining framework that couples local transition learning with recurrent multi-step prediction in a frozen JEPA representation space. A shared inverse dynamics model infers compact continuous latent actions from adjacent observations, while a latent world model recurrently predicts the future JEPA features. Because each predicted feature becomes the context for the next transition, errors at later steps backpropagate through the rollout to earlier latent actions, encouraging temporally coherent dynamics beyond pairwise reconstruction. We transfer this representation to a vision-language model using two complementary objectives: latent distillation from the frozen inverse teacher and recurrent future-feature prediction through the frozen latent world model. The resulting policy is then adapted to robot demonstrations with action flow matching. At deployment, the explicit latent-action and world-model branches are removed, and the fine-tuned VLM predicts physical actions directly, reducing inference complexity. With only 11M pretraining samples and 1.06B trainable parameters, ReLAP achieves 97.9% on standard LIBERO and 70.0% over zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations. On the LARY latent-action benchmark, ReLAP ranks second in both mean regression error and mean classification accuracy among the compared methods. These results demonstrate that recurrent action-free latent action pretraining can learn compact, temporally structured, and transferable representations for downstream robot control.
arxiv:2611.22077.authors: R. Gnana Praveen, Ali Rouzbayani, Zhiying Jiang, Bidhan Roy

arxiv:2611.22908.title: Arboreus: A Realistic Boreal Forest Simulator with Topographic Terrain and Satellite-Informed Parametric Tree Distributions
arxiv:2611.22908.abstract: This work presents Arboreus, a realistic Boreal forest simulator, developed to support statistical validation of robotic autonomy algorithms in Boreal forest environments. Arboreus presents an automated methodology for synthesizing large-scale, data-informed, plausible forest worlds from parametric trees, height-variant terrain, and satellite-informed tree density distributions. The parametric generation of dominant Boreal tree species such as Birch, Spruce, and Pine is guided by trunk, canopy, and foliage parameters, extracted from growth studies in the Nordic areas. Tree distribution in an area of interest is guided by the Copernicus satellite dataset, which provides tree cover density and dominant species type at up to 10m raster resolution. The forest floor generation is guided by topographic data from the Swedish cadastral agency to produce realistic data-informed terrains. Given coordinates and extents of forested areas of interest, Arboreus synthesizes data-informed plausible forests, while offering flexibility to inject user observations of real forests (detail, age, dimensionality and tree count), which is critical for realistic synthetic data generation and for the testing of feature-sensitive autonomy algorithms. The applicability of Arboreus for benchmarking and validation of robot autonomy for different robot mobilities is demonstrated in Gazebosim, Unreal Engine, and Isaac Sim physics engines. The applicability of Arboreus as a source of synthetic forest data and its potential to support downstream forest resource mapping research (volume estimation, tree instance segmentation and stem attribute estimation) is also demonstrated. Arboreus has been open-sourced along with a dataset comprising 25 Boreal forest worlds of size 1000m2 corresponding to three real forest sites.
arxiv:2611.22908.authors: F. Labra Caso, A. Saradagi, A. Koval, G. Nikolakopoulos

arxiv:2611.21789.title: ASTRA: ASV Simulator for Transferable Realistic Autonomy
arxiv:2611.21789.abstract: Autonomy development for marine autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) remains challenging because field testing is costly and difficult to reproduce. Existing marine simulation tools provide mature capabilities in vessel dynamics, robotics integration, and visual rendering, but these strengths are emphasized differently across platforms. This paper presents ASTRA, an ASV simulation framework built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim that combines marine vehicle dynamics, photorealistic perception, and Robot Operating System (ROS 2) autonomy interfaces within a common environment. ASTRA incorporates a Fossen-style marine dynamics model together with geometry-based buoyancy and programmable spectral wave disturbances, enabling non-planar hydrostatic and wave-induced motion. The simulator reproduces the sensor configuration of a physical BlueBoat testbed, including GPS, IMU, LiDAR, and RGB-D sensing exposed through ROS 2. This allows localization, perception, planning, and control software to be developed against interfaces consistent with the physical platform. The BlueBoat's existing ROS 2 localization and perception modules were ported directly into ASTRA, while targeted zero-propulsion experiments were used to verify the implemented wave-body coupling. The simulated roll response was consistent with the expected non-oscillatory hydrostatic behavior, and heave remained highly coherent with the generated wave field, with approximately unity gain at the dominant wave frequency in the tested sea states. ASTRA is intended as an open-source testbed for marine autonomy development, simulation-based benchmarking, and sim-to-real experimentation.
arxiv:2611.21789.authors: Tsimafei Lazouski, Cody Sheltraw, Alan Papalia, Maani Ghaffari

arxiv:2611.23144.title: $π^4$: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion
arxiv:2611.23144.abstract: $π^4$ is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, $π^4$ achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at https://github.com/yyfz/Pi4.
arxiv:2611.23144.authors: Yifan Wang, Weiguang Zhao, Ni Yang, Haoyu Guo, Junting Dong, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen

arxiv:2611.19244.title: Agentic On-Policy Distillation Implicitly Reshapes LLMs' ReAct Patterns
arxiv:2611.19244.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers specialized capabilities to language-model agents, but its cross-domain effects on interaction remain unclear. We investigate how OPD reshapes ReAct interaction patterns across mathematics, ALFWorld, and $τ^2$-bench, focusing on reasoning, actions, and observation acquisition. General-reasoning supervision reduces mathematical tool attempts from 70.4% to 14.4% while increasing accuracy from 16.7% to 38.0%; code-interpreter supervision improves household actions and retail queries. In contrast, ALFWorld supervision reduces $τ^2$-bench accuracy from 41.5% to 6.6%, accompanied by frequent tool calls that violate user-information dependencies. To address negative transfer using only source-domain training trajectories, we explore selective OPD guided by teacher preference changes before and after domain-specific RL. Retaining the top 95% of positions raises $τ^2$ accuracy from 11.5% to 29.9% with a source-learning trade-off.
arxiv:2611.19244.authors: Deyang Kong, Zhaoyi Li, Sijian Ren, Yuan Wei, Ying Wei, Defu Lian, Shikun Zhang, Wei Ye

arxiv:2611.18856.title: Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement
arxiv:2611.18856.abstract: Harness optimization is often studied with a fixed policy model and benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer must decide which parts of an evolved harness to reuse or revise, but the harness alone may not explain why earlier edits were made or how they performed. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), a setting for continuing existing harness-optimization methods across compatible benchmarks or policy models. We propose Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for the harness optimizer, rather than the task-solving policy. SIM groups edits by recurring harness problem and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. New attempts extend this history as optimization continues. In our experiments across four domains, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in cross-dataset and pairwise cross-model comparisons. Across ten independent source runs in coding, paired continuations with SIM improve final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation ($p=0.003$).
arxiv:2611.18856.authors: Xin Yu, Fei Xia, Jiaqi Pan, Youbao Tang, Chengzhi Liu, Adams Yu, Sicong Jiang, Yanfei Chen, Lingzhou Xue, Ting Yu

arxiv:2611.21791.title: Regularized Score Centering
arxiv:2611.21791.abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.
arxiv:2611.21791.authors: Hao Bai, Chenlu Ye, Xuanchang Zhang, Aviral Kumar, Tong Zhang

arxiv:2611.15348.title: Breath-Dx: A Time Series Classification Benchmark for Disease Screening with eNose
arxiv:2611.15348.abstract: Electronic nose (eNose) technology offers a portable, non-invasive route for disease screening via exhaled breath analysis. However, progress in the field is hindered by the lack of systematic benchmarks that compare machine learning methods under realistic conditions, particularly sensor drift, a known but rarely quantified failure mode. Most existing studies rely on small, private datasets with inconsistent protocols, rendering results non-comparable and slowing progress. We introduce Breath-Dx, the first comprehensive benchmark of time series classification methods for breath-based disease screening. Our work leverages the Scent of Health (S-OH) dataset, the largest public clinical eNose collection to date, comprising 1,234 patients across nine diagnostic groups, each providing a 17-channel multivariate time series with explicit temporal train/test splits that account for sensor drift. We systematically evaluate 10 methods spanning four families: feature-based tabular learners, convolution-based models, graph-based, and time series architectures. All methods degrade significantly under temporal validation (0.05-0.12 AUC drop compared to random cross-validation), confirming that drift embeds a strong temporal signal. Under this realistic evaluation, the best methods achieve ROC AUC of 0.74-0.76 for some lung conditions, though others remain near chance. Recurrent architectures show the most consistent performance across diseases, while specialized time series methods achieve the highest peak results. Demographic confounders matter: breath signals provide independent diagnostic value for some conditions but add little beyond age for others. We release the S-OH dataset, all temporal splits, evaluation protocols, and code to enable reproducible research and accelerate progress in clinical breathomics.
arxiv:2611.15348.authors: Ivan Poddiakov, Ivan Kruzhilov, Galina Zubkova, Svetlana Erofeeva, Andrey Savchenko, Pavel Blinov

arxiv:2611.22055.title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
arxiv:2611.22055.abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.

arxiv:2611.19800.title: Multi-Branch Transformer
arxiv:2611.19800.abstract: Transformer language models are commonly scaled by making their blocks wider or stacking them deeper. In this work, we explore a complementary path: branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks. We introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which processes the input through shared initial layers, executes independently parameterized branches of sequential blocks in parallel, and fuses their outputs before shared final layers. At comparable training compute, we study three MBT variants: Wide-Shallow preserves block width, Narrow-Deep preserves sequential depth, and Balanced interpolates between them. In controlled pretraining experiments at four mixture-of-experts scales (0.8B to 2.1B total parameters), 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBTs consistently outperform sequential Transformers under matched parameter and training-compute budgets. Balanced MBTs improve further and retain comparable quality as the number of branches increases. To improve inference efficiency at long contexts, we introduce Joint-KV, which constructs a shared KV cache from branch representations at each depth. Our final recipe combines Balanced MBTs with Joint-KV, supported by an inference engine that exploits branch grouping and shared-cache reuse. Fitted scaling curves indicate that standard Transformers require up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match our final models' validation loss. These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU. Ablation studies show that branching yields gains beyond changes in width and depth, enables an effective KV-sharing strategy (Joint-KV), remains robust across fusion functions, and performs best in the middle layers. These findings show that branching offers a practical path for scaling language models toward both better modeling quality and faster inference.
arxiv:2611.19800.authors: Gaotang Li, Lingjie Chen, Chunyuan Deng, Zhiwei Xu, Hongzheng Chen, Christopher De Sa, Jingrui He, Yingheng Wang, Hanghang Tong

arxiv:2611.20992.title: MedJev: A System One Vision-Language Decision Model for Fast and Effective Medical Image Understanding
arxiv:2611.20992.abstract: Medical image understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) typically relies on autoregressively generating reasoning and answer tokens. These unnecessary tokens make the inference cost scale with the response length and force the answer to be parsed from free-form text, incurring avoidable latency and decision errors. To this end, we introduce \textsc{MedJev}, a \emph{system one} vision-language decision model that maps medical images, questions, and candidate answers directly to decisions in a single multimodal forward pass, without any autoregressive generation process. For fast inference, \textsc{MedJev} removes the upper language layers and the generative output pathway, while keeping the full vision pathway and all visual tokens. On this shortened backbone, a decision head scores each candidate by pretrained query--key matching and refines the scores with a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) residual, coupling the pretrained matching structure with task-specific nonlinear discrimination. Built on Qwen3.5-4B, \textsc{MedJev}-4B improves both accuracy and speed over the original model on each of four medical image classification and visual question answering benchmarks, with an absolute accuracy gain of \textbf{7.93\%} and a \textbf{6.04$\times$} end-to-end speedup. Further comparison with 20 cutting-edge models shows that \textsc{MedJev}-4B achieves state-of-the-art performance and inference speed among 4B--9B general and medical VLMs, indicating that direct multimodal decision making is an effective route to fast and effective medical image understanding.
arxiv:2611.20992.authors: Fan Zhang, Hao Wu, Jinyang Wu, Hongyu Qu, Zheng Lian, Dongfu Yin, Qingsong Wen, Pheng-Ann Heng

arxiv:2611.20441.title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
arxiv:2611.20441.abstract: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.
arxiv:2611.20441.authors: Koki Itai, Jun Hirako, Hiroaki Yamagiwa

arxiv:2611.21412.title: Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in a Nigerian Cohort
arxiv:2611.21412.abstract: High-resolution brain MRI is important for neuroradiological assessment, yet routine clinical protocols often rely on fast, anisotropic 2D acquisitions, particularly in resource-constrained settings. These acquisitions may differ in orientation, alignment and anatomical coverage, resulting in partially overlapping image stacks. Existing learning-based super-resolution methods typically rely on single, under-constrained inputs or fixed multi-stack configurations with idealised acquisition geometry. We introduce MS-HVED, a sequence-agnostic framework for flexible multi-stack brain MRI super-resolution. Available axial, coronal and sagittal stacks are independently encoded into multi-scale Gaussian posteriors and fused using a field-of-view-aware Product-of-Gaussians formulation that limits contributions from unsupported regions. Physics-informed domain randomisation simulates heterogeneous clinical acquisition conditions, including obliqueness, partial coverage and imaging artefacts. MS-HVED achieved competitive or superior reconstruction fidelity across synthetic benchmarks and improved downstream tissue segmentation relative to low-resolution inputs. To assess generalisation beyond the training cohorts, we performed external clinical validation on 30 routine brain MRI examinations from a Nigerian cohort, representing an under-represented population in medical imaging research. These examinations formed the largest component of a blinded reader study involving 44 real cases and seven expert neuroradiologists. In the Nigerian cohort, MS-HVED was preferred over the supervised baseline for overall image quality in 187 of 210 paired assessments. Across all clinical cohorts, MS-HVED achieved higher overall-quality scores with all available inputs (5.93 vs. 4.49, p<.001), with the preference persisting when axial or coronal inputs were omitted (p<.001). Code at github.com/cai4cai/ms-hved
arxiv:2611.21412.authors: Kabir Hamzah Muhammad, Lorena Garcia-Foncillas Macias, Soumya Snigdha Kundu, Emily Guilhem, Jon Cleary, Amal Saleh Nour, Yodit Abraham Yaynishet, Chinasa Kalaiwo, Peter Chibuta, Ugumba Kwikima, Udunna Anazodo, Jonathan Shapey, Tom Vercauteren

arxiv:2611.17610.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
arxiv:2611.17610.abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

arxiv:2611.18330.title: Marimba: A System One Model for Speech
arxiv:2611.18330.abstract: Speech applications require decisions about term presence, turn completion, and language within an audio window. We present Marimba, an interface for typed speech decisions built on frozen Qwen3-ASR 0.6B features. Lexical questions use zero-shot scoring of ASR transcripts; non-lexical questions use a question-conditioned head and a separate layer-18 turn-end readout. Language identification uses the ASR model's own language scores. On private conversational test sets, decoder AUROC is 0.80-0.92; on public read speech it is 0.92-0.97. Speech Commands four-way accuracy is 0.93; binary lexical ECE is at most 0.08. Personal-information detection, which passes the greedy transcript to a private, curated PII pipeline, reaches item-level F1 0.904 on synthetic Brazilian Portuguese speech (1.000 on reference transcripts). Layer-12 speaker readouts detect speaker change with AUROC 0.966-0.980 on AMI and VoxConverse, above an ECAPA baseline, and count speakers (0, 1, 2, or 3+) more accurately than pyannote 3.1. The turn-end readout reaches AUROC 0.930 versus Smart Turn v3.2 at 0.982 on Smart Turn's own test set. On a subset of ICSI meetings labeled by next speaker, AUROC is 0.716 versus 0.712; the paired confidence interval includes zero.

arxiv:2611.20321.title: Unreasonable Confidence from Simulator Misspecification: Directional Robustness on the SPEED+ Sim-to-Real Benchmark
arxiv:2611.20321.abstract: Vision-based navigation systems for orbit must be trained almost entirely on synthetic imagery, because real labelled images of a given spacecraft in flight rarely exist. Benchmarks like SPEED+ are built for that situation: the training set comes from a simulator, and the test sets are real images of a satellite mockup under two kinds of lighting. That simulator approximates how light reflects off mylar and aluminium, and like every scientific simulator it is misspecified. Its error is radiometric, since it misses the specular highlights, hard shadows and sensor saturation common in real images. We probe the resulting synthetic-to-real gap, the central risk for such systems, with a deliberately simple monocular pose estimator. In a 2x2 study of backbone adaptation and photometric augmentation, trained on synthetic images and tested on both real hardware-in-the-loop domains, we find three things. (1) The model does not know it is failing: regions conformally calibrated to 90% on synthetic data cover only 9-15% of rotation errors on sunlamp and 21-38% on lightbox, so a wrong pose carries the confidence of a correct one. (2) Transfer is asymmetric: scaling data and features improved synthetic rotation error from 1.65 to 1.03 rad but moved the harshly lit sunlamp domain by only 0.05 rad, under twice its seed s.d., whereas adapting the backbone's last stage carried 63-83% of its extra synthetic gain to both real domains. (3) Once the backbone adapts, augmentation helps only in the direction it models: our photometric stack improved the diffusely lit lightbox domain from 1.17 to 0.99 rad on every seed but moved sunlamp no more than seed-to-seed variation, while with the backbone frozen it helped sunlamp more. Every post-review experiment was pre-registered, and the code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record are at https://github.com/lokindoo/spacecraft-pose-estimation.

arxiv:2611.23140.title: GameRealm: Grounding Visual Learning in Interactive Games
arxiv:2611.23140.abstract: Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.
arxiv:2611.23140.authors: Weiguang Zhao, Yifan Wang, Ni Yang, Yating Wang, Xingyu Miao, Yankai Jiang, Mulin Yu, Tao Lu, Haoyu Guo, Junting Dong, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen

arxiv:2611.21925.title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding
arxiv:2611.21925.abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.
arxiv:2611.21925.authors: Jameson Sandler, Shane Bergsma, Mostafa Elhoushi, Bin Claire Zhang, Gavia Gray, Joel Hestness, Nolan Dey, Ferdinando Fioretto

arxiv:2611.22563.title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference
arxiv:2611.22563.abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon
arxiv:2611.22563.authors: Oleg Pavlov, Nikita Gavrilov, Soslan Kabisov, Gennadii Savrasov, Andrey Kuznetsov, Anton Konushin, Dmitrii Zhemchuzhnikov

arxiv:2611.22565.title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback
arxiv:2611.22565.abstract: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill
arxiv:2611.22565.authors: Gennadii Savrasov, Artem Slavin, Soslan Kabisov, Andrey Kuznetsov, Anton Konushin, Dmitrii Zhemchuzhnikov

arxiv:2611.21382.title: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0: Evaluating Visual Artifacts under Task Specifications
arxiv:2611.21382.abstract: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.
arxiv:2611.21382.authors: Shuyi Ouyang, Xiaojun Tang, Zijian Zou, Xintong Zhang, Mingli Song, Guannan Zhang, Hongwei Xue

arxiv:2611.21421.title: AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program Specifications via Executable Postconditions
arxiv:2611.21421.abstract: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior. Prior approaches obtain this feedback through explicit proofs or separately implemented code with formal correspondence proofs, both expensive. We introduce AuXSpec, a Lean framework that pairs declarative postconditions with executable counterparts, obtained through type class resolution when possible and otherwise defined separately with an equivalence proof. Test cases can then evaluate declarative specifications by execution, letting us use agreement as a reinforcement-learning reward. Using AuXSpec, we synthesize 3,037 LeetCode problems and expand training to 19.5K samples through expert iteration on Codeforces. Experiments show that training Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B with the execution-based reward improves SpecGen pass@4 on AuXSpec-Test 0.7% $\to$ 82.7% and 14.3% $\to$ 84.3%, and the 27B model outperforms all frontier models. On the out-of-domain Verina benchmark with its original prompts, both models improve 7.0% $\to$ 90.5% and 21.9% $\to$ 90.5% and surpass VeriSpecGen-30B-A3B, the prior state of the art among open-source specification models, on pass@1 (theirs 47.6% vs. ours 73.7% and 84.5%) and pass@4 (theirs 63.9% at pass@10 vs. ours 90.5%). We release the weights of the trained 9B and 27B models and the 3,037 problems with test cases, including the 300-problem AuXSpec-Test benchmark with expert review and correctness proofs for future evaluation. Models and data: https://huggingface.co/collections/eth-algopt/auxspec. Website: https://auxspec.org
arxiv:2611.21421.authors: Haocheng Wang, Weixuan Yuan, Florian Hübler, Yinya Huang, Zhijiang Guo, Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai, Rasmus Kyng

arxiv:2611.19857.title: PanDWM: Panoramic 4D Driving World Models
arxiv:2611.19857.abstract: Driving world models usually generate videos from six pinhole cameras with separate optical centres and small overlaps, and must learn to keep these views consistent. We present PanDWM, which stitches them into one $360^\circ$ panoramic band. Camera boundaries then fall inside one image, so keeping the views consistent means keeping the image continuous, and each pixel still records its camera ray. Conditioned on layouts, a causal student generates the band window by window in four steps; it is distilled from a causal teacher and trained on its own rollouts. A feed-forward decoder lifts each frame along these rays into 3D Gaussians, and static Gaussians from neighbouring frames complete them into 4D scenes. On nuScenes, scored in one stitched $360^\circ$ view, PanDWM has lower FID and FVD than the multi-camera baselines at $8$-$46\times$ their speed, and keeps its 50-step teacher's FID while lowering FVD by 22-25%.
arxiv:2611.19857.authors: Jiajun Sun, Zeyu Zhang, Zeyu Ren, Guangfeng Jiang, Yang Zhao, Hao Tang

arxiv:2611.17048.title: Beyond Answering: Learning to Speak First and Act in Streaming Video
arxiv:2611.17048.abstract: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) lets the model act on what it sees by invoking external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporating returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities.
arxiv:2611.17048.authors: Shuhan Li, Huankang Guan, Xintong Guo, Yang Bo, Yuyang He, Dunyuan Xu, Jingyan Chen, Fang Liu, Tsz Kin Wan, Jinpeng Chen, Zhenqi He, Yuxuan Hu, Wenbo Li, Han Gao, Qijun Li, Long Chen, Hongsheng Li, Rui Liu

arxiv:2611.15671.title: The Noise Floor of a Quantization Comparison: Engine, restart, batch and kernel drift, measured against 8-bit and 4-bit effects in two decision models
arxiv:2611.15671.abstract: A quantized model is usually judged by comparing it with its BF16 original, but that comparison changes more than the weights. It often changes the serving engine, it always runs on a different server instance, it may change how requests are batched, and on some stacks the library selects a different kernel depending only on which packages import. We measure each of these sources on the same 2,400 public decisions for two of Cloudflare's decision models, Clef-flash (9B) and Clef (27B), on an NVIDIA GB10, and state every quantization effect as the excess over them. Sources that are not quantization move between 0 and 0.92% of decisions. llama.cpp restarts are bit-identical on every record for both models. vLLM restarts flip 0, 5 and 20 decisions at BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 on Clef-flash and 4, 0 and 22 on Clef; a third instance of Clef's quantized builds (exploratory) leaves FP8 at 0 and puts NVFP4 at 4 to 22, depending on which two instances are compared. An engine change at BF16 flips 6 to 16, a batch-size change 8 to 15, and the Gated DeltaNet kernel transformers selects unasked 10 to 14. Quantization inside one engine moves more: for Clef-flash and Clef, 0.88% and 1.04% at Q8_0, 2.12% and 1.62% at FP8, 5.79% and 3.50% at Q4_K_M, and 5.79% and 5.67% at NVFP4. On both models, every 4-bit interval excludes every non-quantization source. Two of our five pre-registered predictions failed, and the same two fail when the tests are rerun on the 27B: FP8 is not inside restart noise, and changing engine moves fewer decisions than 8-bit quantization does. Accuracy hides most of this. Over the full 31,275 public questions, Clef's Q4_K_M build moves accuracy by a net six questions (-0.02 points [-0.20, +0.16]) while 436 of its decisions get worse (exploratory), and NVFP4 costs Clef-flash 0.95 points and Clef 0.65. We release the code, quantization recipes, per-record outputs and the pre-registration.

arxiv:2611.21392.title: VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context
arxiv:2611.21392.abstract: Understanding long videos requires locating evidence, resolving visual details, and integrating observations into an answer. Even when relevant evidence is present, performing these operations within long, dense visual sequences burdens both perception and reasoning. Video agents enable selective inspection, but returning frames to the planner still accumulates visual information in its reasoning context. Delegating perception reduces this burden, yet sparse sampling can miss decisive details, and per-frame descriptions can preserve context growth. We introduce VideoNexus, a training-free framework that separates detailed video perception from evidence-driven planning and reasoning. The planner controls where to inspect, what to resolve, and how densely to sample. Perception sub-agents process native audio-video in independent contexts and return compact, temporally grounded evidence for iterative search and verification. Using Gemini 3.8 Flash for both planning and perception, VideoNexus achieves 88.6% accuracy on full LVBench, exceeding same-backbone static ingestion and built-in agentic processing by 3.6 and 1.1 points, respectively, at 44% of the latter's measured API cost. A paired LVBench subset ablation shows lower planner input and higher accuracy. With Kimi K3 as the shared backbone, VideoNexus improves over the official Video-GAIA ReAct harness by 8.5 points in our evaluation. These results support compact evidence exchange for combining detailed observation with efficient planning and reasoning.
arxiv:2611.21392.authors: Yancheng Long, Xuanyu Zheng, Wei Chen, Luoyuan Zhang, Haoyang Xu, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao

arxiv:2611.23034.title: M3OPD-Reasoner: An Open Recipe for Post-Training Multimodal Reasoning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
arxiv:2611.23034.abstract: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) enables a single student to absorb the skills of several domain teachers by learning from its own generated responses. We present Multimodal Model Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation Reasoner (M3OPD-Reasoner), a fully open recipe for post-training vision-language models (VLMs) over three reasoning domains: image STEM, image perception, and video. We curate two datasets, M3OPD-SFT-1.35M for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and M3OPD-RL-193K for reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards. On these data, we compare post-training recipes that start from Qwen3.5-9B: training one model on the mixed data of all domains (MixSFT and MixRL), and training one teacher per domain with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), directly or after an SFT warm-up, and distilling the teachers into one student with MOPD. We evaluate on 21 image STEM, image perception, and video reasoning benchmarks after we decontaminate the training data against them. The comparison establishes MOPD of teachers trained with GSPO directly from Qwen3.5-9B as the best recipe: the student closely matches each teacher on its own domain and is on average above the mixed-training baselines on the same prompts. Since MOPD already merges the domain capabilities that MixRL would otherwise have to learn, its student is a stronger starting point for RL, and we ask whether the same data can carry the model further from there: we add MixRL on top of the MOPD student, on the same prompts and with the same settings, which, to our knowledge, no prior VLM recipe has studied. The same prompts still improve the MOPD student, with no collapse, and give our main model, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B. MOPD and MixRL can therefore work as consecutive stages that get more out of the same data. We release all data, the training code, and the checkpoints of every stage.
arxiv:2611.23034.authors: Nguyen Quang Trung, Hoang Phan, Shuo Sun, Longyin Zhang, AiTi Aw

arxiv:2611.23026.title: TPHC: Improving Hyper-Connections with Tensor-Parallel Grouped Updates
arxiv:2611.23026.abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into $N$ parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts $N\in\{4,8,16\}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.
arxiv:2611.23026.authors: Xinying Hu, You Wu, Haoyi Wu, Jianchao Tan, Kefeng Zhang, Yuchen Xie, Kewei Tu

arxiv:2611.21152.title: From Repositories to Training Environments: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding Agents with Environment Evolution Loop
arxiv:2611.21152.abstract: Training coding agents for long-horizon tasks requires environments with verifiable feedback. Existing pipelines often follow a linear process that ends with validation, establishing usability but providing little guidance on improving training value. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) often requires model rollouts or model training followed by downstream evaluation, with costs and feedback delays amplified on long-horizon tasks. How can we use timely, reliable proxy signals to improve training value and synthesize environments at scale? We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real repositories into verifiable environments where agents build complete projects from scratch given a language specification. Its Environment Evolution Loop optimizes a multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope through proxy feedback. RepoFactory produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, which achieves gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five benchmarks covering long-horizon coding and agentic tasks in real-world production settings, compared with 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution. These results highlight the training value of RepoFactory environments and the additional gains from the Environment Evolution Loop.
arxiv:2611.21152.authors: Yang Tian, Tianyu Zheng, Xiyuan Yang, Yaxin Du, Chengran Yang, Bo Zhao, Jian Yang, Bryan Dai

arxiv:2611.23108.title: FMT: Lossless Image Compression in a Fixed Number of Parallel Steps
arxiv:2611.23108.abstract: Learned lossless codecs make smaller files than common classical codecs, yet the images we archive and train on still use classical codecs. A main reason is time: a learned codec takes seconds to decode a photo that a classical codec opens in milliseconds, and their faster variants give up most of their gain in size. We argue that much of this time is spent waiting, not computing: the network waits for the values it conditions on, and the arithmetic decoder reads them one at a time. We introduce FMT (Fixed-step Multiscale Tree), a lossless image format whose decoding order and entropy coder are designed together so that neither wait grows with the image. FMT stores an image as a coarse-to-fine tree whose steps hold independent values: a GPU predicts each step at once and decodes it in parallel rANS lanes that carry their states from step to step, so an image of any size decodes in a fixed number of sequential steps. On this tree we build a family of bit-exact codecs, from a rule with no network to large networks, and no codec we ran on the same GPU beats any of them on both size and speed. Without a network, FMT beats NVIDIA's HTJ2K on size and speed; with a large one, it decodes Kodak photos 9 to 61X faster than learned codecs we ran on the same A100, at the same size or smaller.

arxiv:2611.17621.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
arxiv:2611.17621.abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.
arxiv:2611.17621.authors: AI Training Platform Team, Bingwei Zhang, Jing Li, Amir Abdullin, Sihang Chen, Xin Chen, Liangjun Feng, Yingmeng Gao, Tao Guo, Junjie Huang, Dongfang Li, Zhanglian Lin, Jiajun Liu, Zekun Liu, Zhengxuan Lu, Xiaodong Luo, Jian Meng, Ivan Nosov, Linyuan Qiu, Weijian Sun, Wanrui Yan, Binfan Zheng, Zhicheng Zhou, Baotian Hu, Min Zhang, Haizhou Li, Zhiquan Luo

arxiv:2611.22115.title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
arxiv:2611.22115.abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend.
